geo_headlines: FUTURES BOUNCE, LED BY CHIPS. S&P 500 futures 7,749.25 (+0.58%) and Nasdaq 100 futures 29,748 (+1.21%) after last week's 5.5% Nasdaq 100 drop. Intel rose about 4% premarket on a JPMorgan upgrade to neutral; Micron, Broadcom, Qualcomm and TSMC traded 2-5% higher (Yahoo Finance). **Goldman traders said AI credit spreads are the widest of the year and Friday's put volume was the second-highest of the year, behind June (CNBC).**

NEOCLOUD CREDIT STRESS. CoreWeave's credit default swaps reached distress levels last week (CNBC); the stock is up about 1% premarket after Friday's 11.9% drop. The Information reported executives expect only 7-10 of hundreds of neocloud operators to survive, with Nvidia backstopping about $20 billion in leases (AI Weekly).

OIL EASES ON RUSSIA WAIVER. Brent $108.45 (-1.3%) after Friday's $109.86 settle, its highest since May; December WTI $98.17 (-0.9%). Trump signed an executive order Friday evening suspending Russia sanctions and waiving proposed tariffs on buyers of Russian oil (Yahoo Finance); the US expects more than 300,000 tonnes of Russian diesel (investingLive). No US strike on Iran was reported; Trump said the US could "soon finish the job" (Iran International).

CHINA BEATS; ASIA MIXED. China's third-quarter GDP grew 4.5% from a year ago vs 4.4% expected, up from 4.3%; September output +5.5%, retail sales +1.1%, fixed investment -7.2% year to date (investingLive). Kospi +1.8% to 5,768.01, Nikkei -0.6% to 64,916.70, Shanghai +0.4%; Hong Kong closed. Indonesia fell more than 5% to its lowest since 2020 on an MSCI downgrade warning (AP).

FRANCE RIOTS WEIGH ON EUROPE. About 550,000 marched Saturday against living costs; protests turned to rioting and looting, with 2,400 arrests and about 1,500 shops hit (Euronews). At the open the Stoxx 600 fell 0.6%, the DAX 0.8% and the CAC 40 0.5%; the euro slipped 0.2%. Unions called a national strike for November 5.

BONDS STEADY NEAR 5.06%. The 10-year is 5.06% this morning (Bloomberg), after closing Friday at 5.09% (Treasury), down about 15bp last week; 2-year 4.74%, 30-year 5.43%. FedWatch, as of Friday 10/16: October hike 18.8%, December 84.8%. Gold $4,187.50. Bitcoin $82,284.58 (+0.3%).

TODAY AND THIS WEEK. 10:00 AM: NAHB homebuilder index, September 32 (Schwab Network). Earnings: Cleveland-Cliffs and Fifth Third before the open; Steel Dynamics and Zions after. Tuesday: housing starts, GE, GM, RTX, Netflix; November WTI expires. Wednesday: VIX expiration, Meta, Tesla, IBM, Texas Instruments. Fed officials are in their quiet period before October 27-28.
client_frame_short: Markets are bouncing this morning after tech's worst week since June: Nasdaq futures are up about 1%, led by the same chip stocks that fell hardest. **One good morning does not settle the AI financing question, so the right response to last week is the same as the right response to today: rebalance, don't chase or flee.** Oil has eased a bit after the White House waived Russia sanctions, China's growth beat expectations, and this week's earnings from Netflix, Meta and Tesla will tell us more than headlines. Long-term plans do not need to change.
client_frame:
If a client calls this morning, the story is a rebound after a rough week, not a change in direction either way.

Where we are: the S&P 500 is about 2% below its October 6 record close after falling 1.95% last week; the Nasdaq 100 fell 5.5%; the Dow rose. This morning S&P futures are up about 0.6% and Nasdaq futures about 1.2%, led by Intel, Micron and other chip makers.

The AI question is still open. Goldman's traders say AI-related credit spreads are the widest of the year, and CoreWeave's default insurance is priced at distress levels. Money is still flowing to AI, but lenders are asking for more, and the weakest borrowers are being sorted out. That is a credit story inside a healthy demand story, and it can take weeks to play out.

Oil: Brent is about $108, down from Friday's five-month high, after the White House suspended Russia sanctions and waived tariffs on buyers of Russian oil to bring fuel prices down. Hormuz attacks remain elevated and there is no deal with Iran, so oil is still the main inflation risk and the reason markets price about an 85% chance of a December Fed hike.

Elsewhere: China grew 4.5%, a bit better than expected, and riots in France knocked European stocks lower this morning.

Why it matters: diversified portfolios handled last week as designed. Bonds paying about 5% cushioned the tech drop, and the Dow rose. Sharp one-week drops in leadership stocks happen inside long bull markets, and selling into them has historically cost more than it saved.

For clients: stay invested, rebalance toward targets, and do not read too much into one up morning or one down week. What would change the view: a 10-year close above 5.40% (Friday 5.09%), a 30-year above 5.75% (Friday 5.43%), or US strikes on Iran that keep Brent well above $105 (now $108.45). Brent is already there; the missing piece is strikes.
